https://www.telegraph.co.uk/business/202.title: Anti-AI doom prophets launch hunger strike outside Google
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/business/202.subtitle: Protester says new technology is ‘extremely dangerous – and the public isn’t even aware of it’
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/business/202.text:
Two weeks ago, outside Google DeepMind’s London headquarters near King’s Cross, Michaël Trazzi sat down with a crudely drawn billboard to begin a one-man protest against “artificial intelligence which threatens human extinction”.
Trazzi declared a hunger strike until Sir Demis Hassabis, DeepMind’s chief executive, agreed to halt the race towards more powerful AI. After two days alone, he was joined by another activist from Amsterdam, Denys Sheremet.
On Thursday, when The Telegraph spoke to him, Sheremet was on day 12 of his protest.
At a separate protest in San Francisco, Guido Reichstadter, co-founder of Stop AI, had reached day 17 of his own hunger strike.
The protests are a stark escalation of a wave of anti-AI activism from campaigners who fear runaway superintelligence could spell humanity’s doom. While plenty of scientists and AI experts have warned of the potential long-term risks from the technology, only a handful of those concerned have taken such drastic action.
“Everyone wants people to protest, but nobody wants to actually do it themselves,” Trazzi tells The Telegraph. “I was like: OK. If nobody else is going to do it, I guess I am the one doing the hunger strike.”
Tech leaders, including Sir Demis of DeepMind, have repeatedly stated that in the near future powerful AI tools could pose potential risks to mankind if misused or in the wrong hands. There are even fears in some circles that a self-improving, runaway superintelligence could choose to eliminate humanity of its own accord.
Since the launch of ChatGPT in 2022, AI leaders have actively encouraged these fears. The DeepMind boss and Sam Altman, the founder of ChatGPT developer OpenAI, both signed a statement in 2023 warning that rogue AI could pose a “risk of extinction”.
Yet they have simultaneously moved to invest hundreds of billions in new AI models, adding trillions of dollars to the value of their companies and prompting fears of a seismic tech bubble.
Activists have accused AI labs of hypocrisy. Reichstadter – a climate, pro-abortion and AI activist – has been protesting outside the office of AI business Anthropic in San Francisco, which has claimed to be focused on safety.
He says: “In reality, they’re trying to kill you and your family.”
Most campaigners for safer AI have expressed their fears through blogs, lectures, interviews or podcasts. Some groups have grown more organised and focused on political lobbying for tighter regulation. Many tech workers have focused their objections specifically on the risks of AI weaponry, often shaded with anti-Israel themes.
But in recent months, grass roots activists have organised more direct action. The campaign group Pause AI has undertaken a series of protests outside the offices of major businesses.
In the UK, the group organised a letter to DeepMind signed by 60 parliamentarians.
For Trazzi, a 29-year-old film-maker and a former AI researcher at Oxford’s Future of Humanity Institute, these protests have not gone far enough.
“I went to film the Pause AI protest on June 30,” he says. “I was inspired by the energy but frustrated that the protest only lasted less than an hour.”
The hunger strike represents a more extreme step. According to Sheremet, a tech worker and Trazzi’s fellow London protester, AI is “extremely dangerous technology – and the public isn’t even aware of it”.
The strikers have yet to get a response from Sir Demis – although this week, a spokesman said: “Safety, security and responsible governance are and have always been top priorities as we build a future where people benefit from our technology while being protected from risk.”
Claims that AI could soon imperil humanity are hotly debated even among those who buy into the idea that the technology could one day pose unexpected risks.
Experts throw around the concept of “p(doom)” – or the probability of an AI extinction event.
This week Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, told an event he believed there was a 25pc chance that “things go really, really bad”. Elon Musk has claimed that AI poses a 10pc to 20pc chance of destroying humanity.
Eliezer Yudkowsky – the founder of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute and something of a celebrity in the world of AI risk – published a book this month called If Anyone Builds It, Everybody Dies, arguing that any pursuit of super-intelligent AI will almost inevitably end apocalyptically.
But there is plenty of scepticism about these dramatic claims. Responding to Yudkowsky’s book this week, Gary Marcus, professor emeritus at New York University, said: “I don’t think anybody should panic.”
He suggested that the risk to humanity is closer to 1pc. Yann LeCun, the head of AI at Meta, has described the concept of AI doom as “BS” and said the idea an AI would seek to wipe out humanity is “preposterous”.
In the UK, the public are no more afraid of AI extinction than they are of other hypothetical apocalypses, ranging from climate change disasters to nuclear war.
Polling last year by Public First found that 36pc of the public thought there was at least a chance of climate change ending humanity, compared to 34pc for nuclear war, 29pc for a pandemic and 23pc for an AI doomsday – the same number that feared an asteroid could obliterate the Earth.
Substantially more are concerned that AI tools could increase unemployment, at 66pc – but this is an order of magnitude different to the concerns of Trazzi and his allies.
Some in the UK tech sector dismiss the concerns of the hunger strikers as a cry for attention. One source says the protesters are “upset that interest in AI safety has diminished at the big labs” and “no one I know is taking it very seriously”.
After an initial spike in interest in AI safety, companies have instead plunged billions into reaching superhuman intelligence as fast as possible. Governments, meanwhile, have dialled back their rhetoric on AI concerns. The UK, for instance, rebranded its AI Safety Institute as the AI Security Institute.
However, Trazzi – who ended his protest after seven days on the advice of a doctor – insists that their message is getting through.
He shares a card given to the protesters by DeepMind staff. It reads: “We really appreciate the work you do and want to let you know it got a lot of people talking in DeepMind.”
For now, however, their protest remains a small one. The Google AI juggernaut rolls on.
